article_title: Let's Chat: Leveraging Chatbot Outreach for Improved Course Performance
citation: Meyer, Katharine, Lindsay C. Page, Catherine Mata, Eric N. Smith, B. Tyler Walsh, C. Lindsey Fifield, Michelle Tyson, Amy Eremionkhale, Michael Evans, Shelby Frost, and Eye Eoun Jung. (2026). Let's Chat: Leveraging Chatbot Outreach for Improved Course Performance. (EdWorkingPaper: 22-564). https://edworkingpapers.com/ai22-564
title: Non-generative AI academic chatbot with TA-supported knowledge base and #quizme practice function
description: A text-based chatbot with non-generative AI capability that sent 2-3 scheduled, customized messages per week (about 40 per semester) to students in large online courses. Messages provided "timely reminders about course requirements", customized feedback on individual progress, connections to academic supports, and an additional communication channel. When students texted in, the bot responded from a pre-programmed knowledge base; low-probability matches were flagged to the course TA, whose manual responses updated the knowledge base. A #quizme function in Government let students request multiple-choice practice quizzes before exams.
requirements: Faculty buy-in and a course TA embedded in both the course and chatbot administration to maintain the knowledge base and review bot responses daily for quality control
Students opted in to receiving text-based communication from the university
constraints: The #quizme function was deployed only in Government, since Microeconomics did not have exams
Messages required timely gradebook information from the TA to customize outreach to students' performance each week
target_learners: Undergraduate students in large-enrollment, asynchronous online courses at a minority-serving public university
target_learning_goals: Connection to academic supports such as tutoring
examples: In a spring 2021 pilot in Government, 90% of end-of-course survey respondents recommended that GSU continue the bot, and weekly digests were redesigned to be customized to students' course performance to date
key_sources: Meyer, Katharine, Lindsay C. Page, Catherine Mata, Eric N. Smith, B. Tyler Walsh, C. Lindsey Fifield, Michelle Tyson, Amy Eremionkhale, Michael Evans, Shelby Frost, and Eye Eoun Jung. (2026). Let's Chat: Leveraging Chatbot Outreach for Improved Course Performance. (EdWorkingPaper: 22-564). https://edworkingpapers.com/ai22-564

article_title: Knowledge-Based Design Requirements for Generative Social Robots in Higher Education
citation: S. Vonschallen, D. Oberle, T. Schmiedel, and F. Eyssel. (2026). Knowledge-Based Design Requirements for Generative Social Robots in Higher Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12873
title: Make privacy-sensitive GSR features optional and student-controlled to guarantee user autonomy
description: Because user-knowledge personalization depends on processing sensitive student data, the article holds that ethical considerations of privacy, consent, and data security are fundamental. User autonomy "should always be guaranteed by making privacy-sensitive features optional and student-controlled", including emotion detection and physical-environment perception, with informed consent required before processing student-related data.
requirements: Students must give informed consent for personal information to be processed, and technical privacy and security standards must be upheld.
constraints: The article notes some participants did not find certain information (e.g., hobbies) useful, and physical-environment perception may infringe on data protection.
target_learning_goals: responsible and ethically appropriate tutoring interactions
examples: Participants stated students need informed consent and the option to deny access to private information; the authors recommend locally deployable models to increase control over sensitive information.
key_sources: S. Vonschallen, D. Oberle, T. Schmiedel, and F. Eyssel. (2026). Knowledge-Based Design Requirements for Generative Social Robots in Higher Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12873

article_title: The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021
citation: Weiqi Xu and Fan Ouyang. (2022). The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-022-00377-5
title: General system theory frames AI-STEM as an organic system of five interdependent elements
description: The review adopts general system theory (GST) as its organizing framework, arguing that a system is greater than the sum of its parts. From this perspective, AI-STEM is viewed as an organic system containing five basic elements: subject (instructor, learner), information (learning content), medium (carrier of information), environment (educational context), and technology (AI techniques as an external element). The framework was operationalized as a coding scheme applied to 63 empirical articles, with Krippendorff's alpha reliability of 0.91 among two raters, to examine how AI integrates with and influences the other elements and their mutual relationships.
requirements: The framework requires identifying the internal elements of the educational system and the functional relationships between them, per the article's holistic principle
constraints: Technology (e.g., AI techniques) is treated as an external element impacting the functions of the educational system, as the article states
target_learners: Instructors and learners in STEM education across kindergarten to higher education
target_learning_goals: Holistic understanding of how AI technologies integrate with STEM educational systems
examples: The authors coded 63 AI-STEM articles on dimensions including instructor involvement, instructional strategy, educational level, sample size, learning outcome, learning content, medium, context, and AI technique
key_sources: Weiqi Xu and Fan Ouyang. (2022). The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-022-00377-5

article_title: Is a Preference for Realism Really Naive After All? A Cognitive Model of Learning with Realistic Visualizations
citation: Skulmowski, A., Nebel, S., Remmele, M., & Rey, G. D. (2022). Is a Preference for Realism Really Naive After All? A Cognitive Model of Learning with Realistic Visualizations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09638-1
title: GSR model: realism as three independently manipulable dimensions of geometry, shading, and rendering
description: The geometry, shading, and rendering (GSR) model is a technical taxonomy of realism grounded in the actual production process of computer-generated imagery in 3D software. It replaces unidimensional realism continua with three dimensions that 'can individually range from simplified to highly realistic', so that each dimension's contribution to realism can be assessed separately. The authors present it as a common terminology for educators, designers, and researchers, exemplified with renderings of the patella created in Blender (Fig. 2).
requirements: Researchers and practitioners must have enough information about learning materials to recreate a particular level of realism, including software packages, plug-ins, and design choices such as whether the same 3D model underlies realistic and schematic versions
constraints: Realism studies usually compare only a few possible combinations of the three dimensions, so results concern specific GSR combinations rather than realism in general
target_learners: designers and researchers of instructional visualizations
target_learning_goals: describing and categorizing the realism of instructional visualizations
examples: Figure 2 exemplifies the model with renderings of the patella varying geometry detail, shading (solid white, color texture, specular), and rendering style (toon with contour line vs. realistic lighting)
key_sources: Skulmowski, A., Nebel, S., Remmele, M., & Rey, G. D. (2022). Is a Preference for Realism Really Naive After All? A Cognitive Model of Learning with Realistic Visualizations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09638-1

article_title: Multivariate genome-wide covariance analyses of literacy, language and working memory skills reveal distinct etiologies
citation: Chin Yang Shapland, Ellen Verhoef, George Davey Smith, Simon E. Fisher, Brad Verhulst, Philip S. Dale and Beate St Pourcain. (2021). Multivariate genome-wide covariance analyses of literacy, language and working memory skills reveal distinct etiologies. npj Science of Learning 6:23. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00101-y
title: GSEM with combined Independent Pathway/Cholesky (IPC) models for multivariate genetic covariance in unrelated individuals
description: GSEM adapts multivariate twin models to genetic relationship matrices (GRMs) from genome-wide SNP data in unrelated individuals, dissecting phenotypic variance into additive genetic (A) and residual (E) factors. Beyond SNP heritabilities and genetic correlations, it identifies underlying genetic factor structures. The article introduces a novel combined IPC model, "enhancing the interpretability of genetic factor structures without a loss of model fit in residual factor structures", and shows unmodeled shared residual variation can strongly affect model fit.
requirements: Genome-wide SNP genotyping of unrelated individuals to derive GRMs
Dense phenotyping with comparable measures across participants
constraints: Population-level phenomena such as assortative mating and dynastic effects can potentially inflate genetic correlations and upward-bias SNP heritability
Lack of independent cohorts with comparable measures prevented direct replication
examples: Applied to ALSPAC youth (N = 6453) across reading fluency, spelling, phonemic awareness, listening comprehension and non-word repetition measures
key_sources: Chin Yang Shapland, Ellen Verhoef, George Davey Smith, Simon E. Fisher, Brad Verhulst, Philip S. Dale and Beate St Pourcain. (2021). Multivariate genome-wide covariance analyses of literacy, language and working memory skills reveal distinct etiologies. npj Science of Learning 6:23. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00101-y

article_title: Generic service integration in adaptive learning experiences using IMS learning design
citation: Luis de-la-Fuente-Valentín, Abelardo Pardo, Carlos Delgado Kloos. (2011). Generic service integration in adaptive learning experiences using IMS learning design. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.12.007
title: Generic Service Integration (GSI): a bidirectional bridge between IMS LD course engines and external Web 2.0 services
description: GSI is an extension of the IMS Learning Design specification that allows conventional third-party Web 2.0 tools to be included in courses defined with IMS LD. The article states it "allows the inclusion of conventional Web 2.0 services (third party tools) in the context of courses defined with IMS LD, and to bidirectionally exchange information among the course flow engine and the third party tools". A GSI layer built on top of an IMS LD-compliant platform offers a fixed API to the engine, while per-service adapters translate the generic vocabulary into each tool's access method. Services are described functionally at authoring time, matched to a catalogue at deployment, and instantiated cleanly per course offering.
requirements: The UoL must contain a GSI description of the third party service in the IMS manifest
The run-time environment must be compliant with both IMS LD and GSI
A GSI adapter module specific to the requested external tool must be installed in the run-time environment
constraints: Services are assumed to behave passively: an event must occur within the course before the engine requests data from the service
Privacy considerations of the data exchange are deferred to other work by the authors
target_learning_goals: adaptive orchestration of learning flows using external Web 2.0 tools
examples: A workshop Unit of Learning adapted its second act based on a questionnaire hosted in Google Forms, with responses mapped to IMS LD properties
key_sources: Luis de-la-Fuente-Valentín, Abelardo Pardo, Carlos Delgado Kloos. (2011). Generic service integration in adaptive learning experiences using IMS learning design. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.12.007

article_title: Generic service integration in adaptive learning experiences using IMS learning design
citation: Luis de-la-Fuente-Valentín, Abelardo Pardo, Carlos Delgado Kloos. (2011). Generic service integration in adaptive learning experiences using IMS learning design. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.12.007
title: Four requirements for integrating external services into reusable adaptive learning flows
description: The article enumerates four requirements that service-integration extensions should fulfil to preserve the spirit of IMS Learning Design: self-containment, adaptability, reusability and interoperability. Self-containment means "All the information required to deploy and enact a learning flow must be included in the Unit of Learning", interpreted as instructions to find and instantiate the service rather than the service itself. Adaptability extends flow adaptation to third-party services in both directions; reusability requires clean per-instance service instantiation; interoperability forbids proprietary protocols.
requirements: Service descriptions must be packaged in the UoL so deployment does not depend on a specific vendor tool
External services must be configurable by course events and must serve as sources of property values
constraints: The current version of IMS LD only supports a simplified mechanism to include external tools, with orchestration independent of events in the external resource
target_learning_goals: designing interoperable, reusable adaptive learning experiences with third-party tools
examples: In the pilot, each course instantiation created a clean Google Forms instance so all students started under the same circumstances
key_sources: Luis de-la-Fuente-Valentín, Abelardo Pardo, Carlos Delgado Kloos. (2011). Generic service integration in adaptive learning experiences using IMS learning design. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.12.007

article_title: Impact of Geometer's Sketchpad on Students Achievement in Graph Functions
citation: Leong Kwan Eu. (2006). Impact Of Geometer's Sketchpad On Students Achievement In Graph Functions. The Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Technology. http://www.mojet.net
title: Geometer's Sketchpad-based instructional activities for graph functions
description: A ten-week set of instructional activities in which Form Six students used Geometer's Sketchpad worksheets, each student with access to one computer equipped with the software, to draw algebraic, trigonometric and absolute value functions. The article states the activities "allowed the students to explore, discover  and investigate the concepts of  graphing of functions". The control group used only textbooks with chalk-and-talk teaching.
requirements: Each student has access to one computer equipped with the Sketchpad software
Activities follow the Form Six mathematics syllabus and curriculum specifications for graph functions
constraints: Evaluated in a single urban Malaysian secondary school with intact Form Six classes
target_learning_goals: Graphing and understanding properties of algebraic, trigonometric, and absolute value functions
examples: Experimental-group students were given time to explore Sketchpad on their own after basic use was taught, while the teacher progressively shared software features over the ten weeks
key_sources: Leong Kwan Eu. (2006). Impact Of Geometer's Sketchpad On Students Achievement In Graph Functions. The Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Technology. http://www.mojet.net

article_title: Effects of Goal-Setting Skills on Students'academic Performance in English Language in Enugu Nigeria
citation: Abe, Iyabo Idowu; Ilogu, Guy Chibuzoh; Madueke, Ify Louisa. (2014). Effects of goal-setting skills on students' academic performance in english language in Enugu Nigeria. New Approaches in Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.7821/naer.3.2.93-99
title: Goal-Setting Procedure Instrument (GSPI)
description: A 20-item questionnaire prepared by the researchers, adapted from the Self-Efficacy Scale by Sherer et al (1982) and made culture-fair by altering items (e.g., 'I like to grow house plants' changed to 'I fix time limit to achieve my goal'). It contains 12 positive and eight negative statements, scored 1-4 with reverse scoring for negatives; total scores range 20-80, with higher scores indicating higher goal-setting ability.
requirements: Used together with baseline Academic Performance Tests to select students scoring below 40 on the average of the two instruments
constraints: Test-retest reliability of .61 and concurrent validity of .62 reported from a pilot with sixteen male and sixteen female students outside the main study groups
examples: Sample items include 'Once I get a goal I don't give up until I achieve it' and 'Failure just makes me try harder'
key_sources: Abe, Iyabo Idowu; Ilogu, Guy Chibuzoh; Madueke, Ify Louisa. (2014). Effects of goal-setting skills on students' academic performance in english language in Enugu Nigeria. New Approaches in Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.7821/naer.3.2.93-99

article_title: The Effect of Learning Geometry Topics of 7th Grade in Primary Education with Dynamic Geometer's Sketchpad Geometry Software to Success and Retention
citation: Kesan, C. & Çalıskan, S. (2013). The effect of learning geometry topics of 7th grade in primary education with dynamic Geometer's Sketchpad geometry software to success and retention. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 12(1). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Geometer's Sketchpad (GSP) dynamic geometry software with Angles and Polygons worksheets
description: An instructional setup combining Geometer's Sketchpad dynamic geometry software with researcher-developed worksheets for the 7th-grade unit Angles and Polygons. Worksheets contained "open-ended and gap-filling types of questions" with clearly stated GSP operations, and were described as "kinds of browser and inquisitive". Students drew, dragged, and changed features of shapes to discover concepts, with the teacher guiding and directing with questions.
requirements: A computer laboratory with a sufficient number of fully equipped computers where students can study comfortably
Teachers trained to use dynamic geometry software with appropriate pedagogical principles
constraints: The authors warn that without teacher training, geometry subjects "might not get further from demonstrating as presentation in this program"
target_learning_goals: Understanding lines, angles, and triangles in the Angles and Polygons unit
Exploring geometric relations and developing geometric intuition
examples: 21 experimental-group students used the worksheets and GSP drafts in a computer laboratory while control students received traditional teaching from the same researcher
key_sources: Kesan, C. & Çalıskan, S. (2013). The effect of learning geometry topics of 7th grade in primary education with dynamic Geometer's Sketchpad geometry software to success and retention. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 12(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1008875

article_title: Improving Students' Van Hiele Level of Geometric Thinking Using Geometer's Sketchpad
citation: Poh Geik Tieng & Leong Kwan Eu. (2013). Improving Students' Van Hiele Level Of Geometric Thinking Using Geometer's Sketchpad. The Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Technology, 2(3). www.mojet.net
title: Geometer's Sketchpad angle-identification activity sequence for Year Three pupils
description: The intervention consisted of six lessons in which Year Three students used two pre-constructed Geometer's Sketchpad activities per angle concept, one on visualizing the angle and one on identifying its properties. The article states the activities were important "for the students to visualize the angles and identify the properties of angles." The control group completed the same six activities without the software. Posttests followed each lesson pair.
requirements: An introductory lesson familiarizing students with the Geometer's Sketchpad before instruction, plus pre-constructed activities
constraints: Pilot work with Year Six pupils showed students "needed more time to get familiar with the software", so the researcher adjusted time and simplified materials for Year 3
target_learners: Year Three primary students (nine years old) learning angles
target_learning_goals: van Hiele Level 1 (visualizing and recognizing angles) and Level 2 (identifying properties of right, acute, and obtuse angles)
examples: Activity 1: Identify the right angles through visualization; Activity 2: Identify the properties of the right angles, repeated for acute and obtuse angles
key_sources: Poh Geik Tieng & Leong Kwan Eu. (2013). Improving Students' Van Hiele Level Of Geometric Thinking Using Geometer's Sketchpad. The Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Technology, 2(3). www.mojet.net. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1086363

article_title: Gamifying Outdoor Social Inquiry Learning with Context-Aware Technology
citation: Morris Siu-Yung Jong, Tom Chan, Vincent Tam and Ming-Tak Hue. (2017). Gamifying Outdoor Social Inquiry Learning with Context-Aware Technology. International Conference Educational Technologies 2017.
title: GPS-supported gamified mobile app for context-aware outdoor social inquiry learning
description: The article describes a mobile application developed to engage and support students pursuing context-aware social inquiry learning in outdoor environments. Based on received GPS signals, "gamified context-aware scaffolds of the App will pop up in accordance with students' physical positions in the real world", engaging and supporting students in accomplishing outdoor inquiry tasks at the fieldtrip site.
requirements: Requires GPS signal reception to trigger location-dependent scaffolds at inquiry spots in the fieldtrip site
constraints: Designed for outdoor fieldtrip environments rather than classroom settings
target_learning_goals: Social inquiry learning: knowledge acquisition about societal issues
key_sources: Morris Siu-Yung Jong, Tom Chan, Vincent Tam and Ming-Tak Hue. (2017). Gamifying Outdoor Social Inquiry Learning with Context-Aware Technology. International Conference Educational Technologies 2017. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED579295

article_title: The Use of Geospatial Technologies Instruction within a Student/Teacher/Scientist Partnership: Increasing Students' Geospatial Skills and Atmospheric Concept Knowledge
citation: Hedley, M. L., Templin, M. A., Czajkowski, K., & Czerniak, C. (2013). The Use of Geospatial Technologies Instruction Within a Student/Teacher/Scientist Partnership: Increasing Students' Geospatial Skills and Atmospheric Concept Knowledge. Journal of Geoscience Education. https://doi.org/10.5408/11-237.1
title: Field campaign data collection protocol using geospatial technologies for urban heat island study
description: Students set up two field research sites (grassy field and paved area) of ideally 30 by 30 m, matching the MODIS satellite swath size. They collected surface temperature data using infrared thermometers, surface conditions, and atmospheric conditions including cloud cover and aerosols. Data were collected ideally within an hour before or after solar noon, converted to Universal Greenwich Time, and entered on the GLOBE Web site. The article states "The students provided ground truthing of data the satellite was collecting." Data were collected for 10 consecutive school days between Thanksgiving and Christmas/winter break 2007.
requirements: GPS coordinates taken so data could be geolocated
infrared thermometer for remote sensing
GPS unit
GIS software
constraints: If the ideal area was not available, the students could still collect the information from smaller sites
If the data were not collected at that ideal time, it was still valuable, and all data collected were time stamped
key_sources: Hedley, M. L., Templin, M. A., Czajkowski, K., & Czerniak, C. (2013). The Use of Geospatial Technologies Instruction Within a Student/Teacher/Scientist Partnership: Increasing Students' Geospatial Skills and Atmospheric Concept Knowledge. Journal of Geoscience Education. https://doi.org/10.5408/11-237.1

article_title: Youth experiences in gender-sexuality alliances predict academic engagement but not disaffection through social-emotional wellbeing.
citation: Poteat, V. P., Calzo, J. P., Yoshikawa, H., Kellogg, D., Marx, R. A., Richburg, A., & Lipkin, A. (2025). Youth experiences in gender–sexuality alliances predict academic engagement but not disaffection through social–emotional wellbeing. Child Development, 96, 847–864. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.14209
title: Gender–sexuality alliances (GSAs) as school clubs supporting LGBTQ+ youth wellbeing and academic engagement
description: Gender–sexuality alliances (GSAs) are school clubs that "provide space for LGBTQ+ youth and their heterosexual cisgender peer allies to mutually support one another and advocate for LGBTQ+ people." They are now in an estimated 44% of U.S. secondary schools. Typically, GSAs meet weekly or biweekly for up to 1 hour during or after the regular school day. During meetings, youth socialize, support one another, discuss issues faced by the LGBTQ+ community, learn about LGBTQ+ affirming resources, or plan and engage in advocacy efforts. This study examined specific experiences within GSAs—peer responsiveness, advisor responsiveness, and leadership—as predictors of wellbeing and academic outcomes.
requirements: GSAs require adult advisors who are teachers, counselors, or other school staff, and aspire to be youth-led with advisor support.
constraints: The article notes that GSAs are not expressly academically oriented clubs, unlike other school clubs that center on academic interests, accomplishments, or service.
target_learners: LGBTQ+ youth ages 11–22 in secondary school
key_sources: Poteat, V. P., Calzo, J. P., Yoshikawa, H., Kellogg, D., Marx, R. A., Richburg, A., & Lipkin, A. (2025). Youth experiences in gender–sexuality alliances predict academic engagement but not disaffection through social–emotional wellbeing. Child Development, 96, 847–864. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.14209
